why.support: Emails get things done. A clear, polite email gets an answer. A messy one gets ignored.
why.core: Emails and letters get things done: asking for work experience, sorting out your pay, booking an appointment, making a complaint. The right email, written the right way, gets you the right answer. The wrong one gets ignored.
why.extend: Formal emails and letters are among the most common workplace and everyday texts. Their structure and conventions (a clear subject, purpose up front, specific details, a polite request and a professional sign-off) determine whether they achieve their purpose.

articles.title: Emails that get answers

body.support:
A good email is short, clear and polite. It says what you need.

**Who is it for?** A boss or a business needs a **formal** email. Polite. A friend gets a **casual** one.

**The parts**

1. **Subject line:** what it's about. *“Pay query: week of 3 March”*.
2. **Greeting:** *“Dear Ms Lee,”* or *“Hi Sam,”*.
3. **Why you're writing:** say it first. *“I'm writing to ask about my pay.”*
4. **Details:** dates, times, amounts.
5. **What you want, and by when.**
6. **Sign-off:** *“Thanks,”* and your name and phone number.

**Plan, write, check**

- Plan: who's it for? What do you want?
- Write it.
- Check: capitals, full stops, spelling. No “u” or “thx”.

**Stay calm.** Even if you're angry. Calm emails get answers.
body.core:
A good email is short, clear and polite, and it tells the reader exactly what you need. Here's how.

**Know your audience.** Who are you writing to? A boss, a teacher, a council or a business needs a **formal** email: polite and professional. A friend gets a **casual** one. Don't mix them up: “hey u there?” won't get your pay fixed.

**The parts of a formal email**

1. **Subject line:** what it's about, in a few words. *“Pay query: week of 3 March”*, not *“Question”*.
2. **Greeting:** *“Dear Ms Lee,”* or *“Hi Sam,”* if that's how you normally talk to them.
3. **Purpose:** say why you're writing, in the first sentence. *“I'm writing to ask about my pay for the week of 3 March.”*
4. **Details:** the facts they need: dates, times, amounts, order numbers. Use short paragraphs.
5. **Request:** exactly what you want, and by when. *“Could you please check this and let me know by Friday 14 March?”*
6. **Sign-off:** *“Kind regards,”* or *“Thanks,”* then your full name and phone number.

**Plan, draft, edit**

- **Plan:** who's it for? What do you want? What details do they need?
- **Draft:** write it out. Don't worry about perfect yet.
- **Edit:** cut extra words. Make the request clear. Then **proofread**: capitals, full stops, spelling, no text-speak.

**Keep it calm.** Even if you're angry, stay polite and stick to the facts. Angry emails get defensive answers. Calm ones get results.

**One last check.** Would you be happy if this email was forwarded to someone else? If yes, hit send.
body.extend:
Effective emails are concise, specific and courteous, and they make the reader's next step obvious.

**Register.** Match the style to your audience. Employers, institutions and businesses expect a **formal** register: polite, professional and free of slang. Friends and family can receive **casual** messages. Using the wrong register undermines your purpose.

**Structure of a formal email**

1. **Subject line:** specific and informative (*“Pay query: week of 3 March”*).
2. **Greeting:** appropriate to the relationship (*“Dear Ms Lee,”*).
3. **Purpose:** stated in the opening sentence.
4. **Details:** the facts the reader needs (dates, hours, amounts, reference numbers) in short paragraphs.
5. **Request:** precise, with a reasonable deadline.
6. **Sign-off:** courteous, with your full name and contact details.

**Process.** **Plan** (audience, purpose, details), **draft** without over-editing, then **revise** for clarity and concision. Finally, **proofread** for capitals, punctuation, spelling and paragraphing.

**Tone.** Stay calm and factual, even when you're frustrated. Measured emails invite cooperation; hostile ones invite defensiveness.

**Final test.** Would you be comfortable if the email were forwarded to a manager or official? If so, send it.

caseStudies.title: Getting back what you're owed

body.support:
Lots of people get underpaid. In **2024–25**, the **Fair Work Ombudsman** got back **$358 million** for underpaid workers. That's more than **249,000** people.

Young workers are more likely to be underpaid.

The first step is often a clear email to your boss. Legal centres say:

- work out what you should have been paid
- write to your boss with the details: dates, hours, amount
- ask them to pay it, for example within 14 days
- say you'll contact the Fair Work Ombudsman if they don't.

You can call the Fair Work Ombudsman on **13 13 94**.

A clear email is often the fastest fix. It also gives you a record.
body.core:
Lots of Australians get underpaid. The **Fair Work Ombudsman** is the government body that checks pay at work. In **2024–25**, it got back **$358 million** for more than **249,000** underpaid workers.

It said **young workers** made up more than their share of the anonymous reports it got. Young people are more likely to be underpaid. They're also less likely to know what to do.

Often, the first step is a clear, written message to your boss. Legal centres, like Redfern Legal Centre, say you should:

- **work out** what you should have been paid, and what you were paid
- **write to your employer**, setting out the details: dates, hours and the amount
- **ask** them to pay it within a reasonable time, such as 14 days
- **say what you'll do** if they don't, such as contacting the Fair Work Ombudsman.

If that doesn't work, you can contact the Fair Work Ombudsman on **13 13 94**. Generally, you have up to six years to claim unpaid wages.

A calm, clear email won't fix every problem. But it's often the fastest fix. It also gives you a written record if you need help later.
body.extend:
Underpayment is common. In **2024–25**, the **Fair Work Ombudsman** (FWO) recovered **$358 million** for more than **249,000** underpaid workers.

The FWO said **young workers**, who can be easy to exploit, were over-represented in the anonymous reports it received.

A written request is often the first step. Legal centres such as Redfern Legal Centre advise workers to:

- **calculate** what they should have been paid and what they received
- **write to the employer** with specific details (dates, hours and the amount owed)
- **request payment** within a reasonable period, such as 14 days
- **state the next step** if payment isn't made, such as contacting the FWO.

If the issue isn't resolved, workers can contact the FWO on **13 13 94**. There is generally a six-year limit for claiming unpaid wages.

A clear email won't solve every dispute. But it's often the quickest fix. It also creates a written record that can support a later claim.

teacher.overview: Students learn the structure and conventions of formal emails and letters (subject line, greeting, purpose first, details, request with a deadline, sign-off), choose a formal or casual register for the audience, and plan, draft, edit and proofread. They annotate a model email, sort and fix email lines, then draft and send a real email (or a practice one to the teacher). The case study is underpayment: in 2024–25 the Fair Work Ombudsman recovered $358 million for more than 249,000 underpaid workers, and young workers were over-represented in anonymous reports. A clear written request to the employer is often the first step.
prep: Decide what students can send for real (work experience requests, questions to businesses or councils) and what goes to you as practice.
Make sure students have access to an email account (school or personal).
Optional: have the Fair Work Ombudsman's pay calculator or young workers pages ready.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** formal is polite and professional for work, officials and businesses; casual is relaxed for friends. Subject, greeting, purpose, details, request, sign-off. Capitals, full stops, spelling, no text-speak.

**Email:** 1 subject line; 2 greeting; 3 purpose first; 4 details with proof; 5 request with deadline; 6 sign-off with name and number.

**Sort:** “Question” — fix; “hey” — fix; purpose line — good; “u owe me $$$” — fix; request with deadline — good; sign-off — good.

**Fix the email (examples):** “I believe I was underpaid last week.” · “Could you please call me on 0400 000 000?” · “Thank you for your help. Kind regards, [name]” · “I'd appreciate it if this could be resolved by [date].”

realityCheck: **Students may not have a real reason yet.** A work experience request is a great default.
**Privacy.** Don't ask students to share personal pay details; use the made-up example.
**Replies take time.** Let students record a reply later.
**Works in a real class:** yes. Students use this skill straight away, often for work.
